MScFE 660 — Risk Management | Group Work Project 1¶

Crude Oil Price Forecasting using Probabilistic Graphical Models¶

Course: MScFE 660 Risk Management
Data Sources: FRED (Federal Reserve), Yahoo Finance, EIA API v2
Period: January 2010 – December 2024

Setup Instructions¶

  1. Open in Google Colab
  2. Add your API keys: Runtime → Secrets
    • FRED_API_KEY — get free at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/api_key.html
    • EIA_API_KEY — get free at https://www.eia.gov/opendata/register.php
  3. Run all cells top to bottom (Runtime → Run all)

Step 2 — Problem Formulation¶

The author, Alvi, D.A. (2018), aims to forecast crude oil price using Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs). Different Python packages along with a probabilistic framework were utilized to study the graphical structure of crude oil price based on various data resources available online. The thesis targets to solve three main challenges:

  1. To investigate the complexity of oil market's structure, which is contingent on various macroeco-nomic indicators and factors,

  2. To explore and exploit oil market data and gain insights, and

  3. To validate the performance and reliability of the constructed model to apply in real financial markets.

Crude oil plays a crucial role in the global economy. It is widely traded and yet complex. No more explanation is needed as we can vividly observe and feel the tension happening around the world due to the US-Iran conflict recently.

References: Alvi, D.A. (2018). Application of Probabilistic Graphical Models in Forecasting Crude Oil Price. UCL Dissertation. arXiv:1804.10869. Koller, D. & Friedman, N. (2009). Probabilistic Graphical Models: Principles and Techniques. MIT Press.

Support Functions¶

In [3]:
# Resample Series to monthly
def to_monthly(s, label='series'):
    s = s.dropna()
    s.index = pd.to_datetime(s.index)
    s = s.resample('MS').last().ffill()
    print(f"  {label}: {len(s)} monthly obs  [{s.index[0].date()} → {s.index[-1].date()}]")
    return s


def fetch_eia_steo(series_id, api_key, label='EIA series'):
    """
    Pull a monthly EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) series.
    Returns a pandas Series indexed by month-start timestamps.
    Raises ValueError if the series returns no data.
    """
    url = 'https://api.eia.gov/v2/steo/data/'
    params = {
        'api_key': api_key,
        'frequency': 'monthly',
        'data[0]': 'value',
        'facets[seriesId][]': series_id,
        'start': START[:7],
        'end':   END[:7],
        'sort[0][column]': 'period',
        'sort[0][direction]': 'asc',
        'length': 500,
        'offset': 0,
    }
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    rows = r.json()['response']['data']
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError(f"No data returned for series ID: '{series_id}' — check the ID at https://www.eia.gov/opendata/browser/steo")
    s = pd.Series(
        {pd.Timestamp(row['period'] + '-01'): float(row['value']) for row in rows},
        name=series_id
    )
    s.index.name = 'date'
    print(f"  {label}: {len(s)} monthly obs  [{s.index[0].date()} → {s.index[-1].date()}]")
    return s


def safe_eia(series_id, api_key, label):
    """Wrapper: returns None instead of crashing if a series ID is wrong."""
    try:
        return fetch_eia_steo(series_id, api_key, label)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  WARNING — skipped '{label}': {e}")
        return None


def fetch_yf_monthly(ticker, label='ticker'):
    raw = yf.download(ticker, start=START, end=END, interval='1mo', progress=False, auto_adjust=True)
    s = raw['Close'].squeeze()
    s.index = pd.to_datetime(s.index).to_period('M').to_timestamp()
    s = s.dropna()
    print(f"  {label}: {len(s)} monthly obs  [{s.index[0].date()} → {s.index[-1].date()}]")
    return s

Step 5: Data Cleaning¶

In [6]:
df = df_raw.copy()

# Extreme Outlier Detection
print("=== Extreme Outlier Detection (3×IQR winsorisation) ===")
outlier_log = []
for col in df.columns:
    series = df[col].dropna()
    Q1, Q3 = series.quantile(0.25), series.quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower, upper = Q1 - 3 * IQR, Q3 + 3 * IQR
    mask = (df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)
    n_out = int(mask.sum())
    if n_out > 0:
        outlier_log.append({'Variable': col, 'N_outliers': n_out,
                            'Lower_bound': round(lower, 3), 'Upper_bound': round(upper, 3)})
        df[col] = df[col].clip(lower, upper)
        print(f"  {col:20s}: {n_out} extreme value(s) winsorised → [{lower:.2f}, {upper:.2f}]")

if not outlier_log:
    print("  No extreme outliers detected beyond 3×IQR threshold.")



# Bad Data Detection
print("=== Bad Data Detection ===")

# Check for negative prices
price_cols = [c for c in ['WTI_Spot', 'WTI_Futures', 'Brent'] if c in df.columns]
for col in price_cols:
    neg_count = int((df[col] < 0).sum())
    if neg_count > 0:
        print(f"  {col}: {neg_count} negative price(s) — flagged for review")
        # Note: April 2020 WTI futures briefly went negative (CL=F)
        # We keep this as a legitimate data point but flag it
    else:
        print(f"  {col}: no negative prices found")

# Check for duplicate timestamps
dups = int(df.index.duplicated().sum())
print(f"\n  Duplicate timestamps: {dups}")
df = df[~df.index.duplicated(keep='first')]

# Flag unusually large price moves in WTI
wti_chg = df['WTI_Spot'].pct_change()
threshold = wti_chg.std() * 3
large_moves = wti_chg[wti_chg.abs() > threshold].dropna()
print(f"\n  WTI Spot months with |return| > {threshold*100:.1f}% (3σ threshold):")
if len(large_moves) == 0:
    print("  None detected.")
else:
    for dt, val in large_moves.items():
        print(f"    {dt.strftime('%Y-%m')}: {val*100:+.1f}%  ← large move (kept, event-driven)")

print()

# Missing Value Imputation
print("=== Missing Value Imputation ===")
print(f"  Missing values before imputation:\n{df.isnull().sum()[df.isnull().sum() > 0].to_string()}")

# Linear interpolation, orward/backward fill
df = df.interpolate(method='time', limit_direction='both')
df = df.ffill().bfill()

df.to_csv(f'{DATA}/df_gwp1.csv')
print(f"\n Saved: {DATA}/df_gwp1.csv")

    )
    df_raw['GPR_Index'] = gpr.reindex(df_raw.index)

    if 'GPR_Index' not in ALL_VARS:
        ALL_VARS.append('GPR_Index')
    print("  GPR_Index added to dataset ✓")
    print(f"  Mean GPR: {gpr.mean():.1f}  |  Max GPR: {gpr.max():.1f} ({gpr.idxmax().strftime('%Y-%m')})")
except Exception as e:

# Step 5 Bad Data Detection
print("=== Enhanced Bad Data Detection ===")

price_cols = [c for c in ['WTI_Spot', 'WTI_Futures', 'Brent'] if c in df.columns]

for col in price_cols:
    neg_mask = df[col] < 0
    neg_count = int(neg_mask.sum())
    if neg_count > 0:
        print(f"  {col}: {neg_count} negative price(s) detected:")
        for dt in df.index[neg_mask]:
            print(f"    {dt.strftime('%Y-%m')}: {df.loc[dt, col]:.3f} — flagged")
    else:
        print(f"  {col}: no negative prices found ✓")

# Verify April 2020 event is logged explicitly
print("\n  April 2020 WTI event check:")
apr2020 = pd.Timestamp('2020-04-01')
if apr2020 in df.index:
    print(f"    WTI_Spot  2020-04: ${df.loc[apr2020,'WTI_Spot']:.2f}/bbl")
    if 'WTI_Futures' in df.columns:
        print(f"    WTI_Futures 2020-04: ${df.loc[apr2020,'WTI_Futures']:.2f}/bbl")
    print("    Decision: retained — legitimate COVID demand shock (economically meaningful)")

# Duplicate index check
dups = int(df.index.duplicated().sum())
print(f"\n  Duplicate timestamps: {dups} {'✓' if dups==0 else '← removed'}")

# Stale data check: consecutive identical monthly values (possible bad feed)
print("\n  Stale-data check (5+ consecutive identical values):")
found_stale = False
for col in df.columns:
    s = df[col].dropna()
    run = (s != s.shift()).cumsum()
    run_len = run.map(run.value_counts())
    stale_mask = run_len >= 5
    if stale_mask.any():
        found_stale = True
        starts = s[stale_mask & (s != s.shift())].index
        for st in starts:
            print(f"    {col}: {run_len[st]}-month run of {s[st]:.3f} starting {st.date()}")
if not found_stale:
    print("  No stale runs detected ✓")

    ax     = axes_flat[i]
    data_v = df[var].dropna()
    ax.hist(data_v, bins=36, color=color, alpha=0.6, density=True, edgecolor='none', label='Observed')
    mu, sg = data_v.mean(), data_v.std()
    xs     = np.linspace(data_v.min(), data_v.max(), 300)
    ax.plot(xs, stats.norm.pdf(xs, mu, sg), 'k--', lw=1.8, label='Normal fit')
    ax.set_title(var.replace('_', ' '))
    sk = data_v.skew()
    ku = data_v.kurtosis()
    ax.text(0.97, 0.95, f'μ={mu:.2f}\nσ={sg:.2f}\nSkew={sk:.2f}\nKurt={ku:.2f}',
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='top', fontsize=8,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='white', alpha=0.6))
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.35)

# Hide unused subplot slots
for j in range(n_plots, len(axes_flat)):

for ax, (col, title), color in zip(axes.flatten(), macro_vars, macro_colors):
    ax2 = ax.twinx()
    ax.plot(df.index, df[col], color=color, lw=1.6, label=title)
    ax.fill_between(df.index, df[col].min(), df[col], alpha=0.07, color=color)
    ax2.plot(df.index, df['WTI_Spot'], color='grey', lw=0.9, linestyle='--',
             alpha=0.6, label='WTI Spot (right)')
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.35)
    valid = df[[col, 'WTI_Spot']].dropna()
    r_val, p_val = stats.pearsonr(valid[col], valid['WTI_Spot'])
    direction = '↑' if r_val > 0 else '↓'
    ax.text(0.03, 0.93, f'ρ = {r_val:.3f} {direction}  (p = {p_val:.3f})',
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=8.5, color=color)
    lines1, labs1 = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
    lines2, labs2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
    ax.legend(lines1 + lines2, labs1 + labs2, fontsize=7.5, loc='lower right')
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter('%Y'))

In [16]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(17, 10))
fig.suptitle('Return Distribution & Stylized Facts — WTI Crude Oil',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')

# (a) Histogram + Normal + Student-t fits
ax = axes[0, 0]
xs = np.linspace(ret_clean.min(), ret_clean.max(), 400)
mu_r, sg_r = ret_clean.mean(), ret_clean.std()
ax.hist(ret_clean, bins=40, density=True, color='steelblue', alpha=0.55, label='Observed')
ax.plot(xs, stats.norm.pdf(xs, mu_r, sg_r), 'k--', lw=1.8, label='Normal')
t_params  = stats.t.fit(ret_clean.values)
nu_est    = min(float(t_params[0]), 30.0)
ax.plot(xs, stats.t.pdf(xs, nu_est, t_params[1], t_params[2]),
        'r-', lw=1.8, label=f'Student-t (ν={nu_est:.1f})')
ax.set_title('Return Distribution')
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.35)

# (b) Q-Q Plot
ax = axes[0, 1]
qq = stats.probplot(ret_clean.values, dist='norm', fit=True)
theoretical, sample_q = qq[0][0], qq[0][1]
slope_q, intercept_q  = qq[1][0], qq[1][1]
ax.scatter(theoretical, sample_q, s=14, color='steelblue', alpha=0.7, label='Sample quantiles')
ax.plot(theoretical, slope_q * theoretical + intercept_q, 'r-', lw=1.8, label='Normal reference')
ax.set_xlabel('Theoretical Quantiles')
ax.set_ylabel('Sample Quantiles')
ax.set_title('Q-Q Plot (Normal check)')
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.35)

# (c) ACF of returns

Step 9a - Probabilistic Graphical Models¶

Overview¶

Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM) Inspired by Probability theory and Graph theory, Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs) demonstrate graphical results that show the dependent of variables based on their joint probability distribution. Variables will be demonstrated as vertices (nodes) and the dependencies will be represented as the edges of the graph. The purpose of a BN is to demonstrate casual relationships among random variables. Each circle represents something that can be different, a $random variable, prices of stocks, oil, and other commodities, or testing the result of a stock price.

The magic of the graph is that missing lines also tell you something important. When two circles are not connected by an edge, it means that once you know the value of some other circles, those two become independent. They don’t affect each other anymore. This is called Conditional Independence. Because the graph shows only the necessary connections, the model is both fast for computers and easy to use and easy for humans to understand.

PGMs directed (with arrows) and undirected (with plain lines). We focus on the directed kind.

Belief Networks (Bayesian Networks)

Bayesian Networks (or belief networks) uses Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to demonstrate the relationships of random variables. As convention of a DAG,

  • Directed means every edge has an arrow; and
  • Acyclic means you cannot follow the arrows and loop back to where you started (no circular causes).

In a DAG, each node has arrows pointing into it from its parents, the direct causes. The whole joint probability distribution (the chances of everything together) is broken down into a product of smaller, simpler pieces

$$P(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_m) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(X_i \mid \text{pa}(X_i))$$

where $pa(Xᵢ)$ represent $X_i$'s parent nodes. The relationship between the nodes and their parents will be explained in a Conditional Probability Table (CPT). The nodes have direct relationships with their parents and are independent of their non descendants.

Markov Networks (Markov Random Fields)

While BNs use arrows to show cause and effects, a Markov Network uses undirected edges, which are lines without arrowheads. This kind of graph represents mutual relationships, not directional ones. Instead of specifying the probability of this variable given its parents, a Markov Network defines the joint probability distribution using potential functions over groups of variables called cliques. The formula looks like this;

$$P(X_1, \ldots, X_m) = \frac{1}{Z} \prod_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \phi_c(X_c)$$

While BNs represent casual relationships, Markov Networks represent symmetry and cyclic constrains among the variables. Hence, BNs would be more appropriate to investigate the casual relationships that affect oil prices.

References: Koller, D. & Friedman, N. (2009). Probabilistic Graphical Models. MIT Press, Chapters 2 - 4. Pearl, J. (1988). Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems. Morgan Kaufmann.

Steps 9 - 10: Inferred Causality Algorithm¶

# Partial correlation helper
def partial_corr(x_var, y_var, cond_set, data):
    """
    Compute partial correlation of x_var and y_var, controlling for
    all variables in cond_set. Uses OLS residual method.
    Returns (correlation, p-value).
    """
    cols = [x_var, y_var] + list(cond_set)
    sub  = data[cols].dropna()
    if len(sub) < 15:
        return 0.0, 1.0
    if len(cond_set) == 0:
        r, p = stats.pearsonr(sub[x_var].values, sub[y_var].values)
        return float(r), float(p)
    Z = np.column_stack([sub[z].values for z in cond_set] + [np.ones(len(sub))])
    res_x = sub[x_var].values - Z @ lstsq(Z, sub[x_var].values, rcond=None)[0]
    res_y = sub[y_var].values - Z @ lstsq(Z, sub[y_var].values, rcond=None)[0]
    if res_x.std() < 1e-12 or res_y.std() < 1e-12:
        return 0.0, 1.0
    r, p = stats.pearsonr(res_x, res_y)
    return float(r), float(p)


# Inferred Causality skeleton learner
def inferred_causality(data, variables, alpha=0.05):
    """
    Constraint-based causal structure learning (PC-style algorithm).

    Phase 1 — Markov Blanket estimation:
        Learn an initial neighbourhood for each variable using pairwise marginal independence tests.

    Phase 2 — Skeleton learning:
        For each adjacent pair, test conditional independence conditioning
        on subsets drawn from the union of their Markov blankets.
        Remove the edge if a separating set is found.

    Phase 3 — V-structure orientation:
        For each triple (Xi — Xk — Xj) where Xi and Xj are not adjacent,
        orient Xi -> Xk <- Xj if Xk is not in the separating set of (Xi, Xj).

    Parameters
    ----------
    data      : pd.DataFrame, columns = variables
    variables : list of column names
    alpha     : significance threshold for independence tests

    Returns
    -------
    edges    : set of frozensets — undirected skeleton edges
    sep_sets : dict mapping frozenset(Xi, Xj) -> separating set
    v_structs: dict of v-structure orientations
    """
    # Phase 1: Markov Blanket
    print("  Phase 1 — Markov Blanket estimation")
    adj = {v: set() for v in variables}
    for i, vi in enumerate(variables):
        for j, vj in enumerate(variables):
            if i >= j:
                continue
            _, pval = partial_corr(vi, vj, [], data)
            if pval < alpha:
                adj[vi].add(vj)
                adj[vj].add(vi)

    mb = {v: set(adj[v]) for v in variables}
    for v in variables:
        print(f"    MB({v:18s}): {sorted(mb[v])}")

    # Phase 2: Skeleton — remove edges with a conditional separating set
    print("\n  Phase 2 — Skeleton learning")
    edges    = set()
    sep_sets = {}
    for i, vi in enumerate(variables):
        for j, vj in enumerate(variables):
            if i >= j:
                continue
            _, p0 = partial_corr(vi, vj, [], data)
            if p0 >= alpha:
                sep_sets[frozenset([vi, vj])] = set()
                continue
            found = False
            candidates = (mb[vi] | mb[vj]) - {vi, vj}
            for vk in candidates:
                _, pc = partial_corr(vi, vj, [vk], data)
                if pc >= alpha:
                    found = True
                    sep_sets[frozenset([vi, vj])] = {vk}
                    break
            if not found:
                edges.add(frozenset([vi, vj]))

    print(f"   Skeleton edges: {len(edges)}")
    for e in sorted([sorted(list(x)) for x in edges]):
        print(f"      {e[0]:20s} — {e[1]}")

    # Phase 3: Orient v-structures
    print("\n  Phase 3 — V-structure orientation")
    v_structs = {}
    for vk in variables:
        nb_k = [e for e in edges if vk in e]
        for ea in nb_k:
            for eb in nb_k:
                if ea == eb:
                    continue
                vi_n = (set(ea) - {vk}).pop()
                vj_n = (set(eb) - {vk}).pop()
                if frozenset([vi_n, vj_n]) not in edges:
                    ss = sep_sets.get(frozenset([vi_n, vj_n]), set())
                    if vk not in ss:
                        v_structs.setdefault(vk, []).append((vi_n, vk, vj_n))
                        print(f"    V-structure: {vi_n} → {vk} ← {vj_n}")

    return edges, sep_sets, v_structs


# Run on a subset of variables (computationally tractable)
